We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

 KType u_1 =Eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → PropThe equality relation. It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system
in specific circumstances.

and it is questionable whether making `Nat.prime` a class is desirable at all.

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```

Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.

```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.

respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.

Warning: this can easily be abused. See the rest of this docstring for details.

Certain propositions should not be treated as a class globally,
but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system
in specific circumstances.

For example, `ZMod p` is a field if and only if `p` is a prime number.
In order to be able to find this field instance automatically by type class search,
we have to turn `p.prime` into an instance implicit assumption.

On the other hand, making `Nat.prime` a class would require a major refactoring of the library,
and it is questionable whether making `Nat.prime` a class is desirable at all.
The compromise is to add the assumption `[Fact p.prime]` to `ZMod.field`.

It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

Certain propositions should not be treated as a class globally,
but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system
in specific circumstances.

For example, `ZMod p` is a field if and only if `p` is a prime number.

we have to turn `p.prime` into an instance implicit assumption.

and it is questionable whether making `Nat.prime` a class is desirable at all.
The compromise is to add the assumption `[Fact p.prime]` to `ZMod.field`.

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```

Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion

```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.

That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.

```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)

  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)

  h1 ▸ h2
```
```

  h1 ▸ h2
```

Infinite-place classification for abstract quadratic fields (exists_totallyReal_or_totallyComplex). The result uses the squarefree-parameter classification to choose a standard model, applies the sign computation there, and transports total reality or total complexity back across the algebra equivalence.

Classification of quadratic fields by squarefree parameters (exists_algEquiv_qsqrtd). Every abstract quadratic field is \mathbb{Q}-algebra-equivalent to Qsqrtd d for some squarefree integer d \ne 1, packaging the parameter normalization into a single existence statement.

Abstract quadratic fields (QuadraticField). QuadraticField K is the project-level property that a field over \mathbb{Q} is a quadratic extension. It is the abstract object of study; the standard model is a coordinate chart. The class wraps Algebra.IsQuadraticExtension ℚ K, so abstract statements can use [QuadraticField K] while still interoperating with mathlib's degree-two API.

Abstract splitting predicates (Splitting.IsSplitAt, Splitting.IsInertAt, Splitting.IsRamifiedAt). The trichotomy for an abstract quadratic field K is exposed by predicates IsSplitAt K p, IsInertAt K p, and IsRamifiedAt K p, removing the need to fix a coordinate model when stating the local behavior of a rational prime.

Abstract splitting trichotomy (split_or_inert_or_ramified_of_quadraticField). Every rational prime is split, inert, or ramified in an abstract quadratic field, by transporting the standard-model trichotomy across the squarefree-parameter classification.

Admissible parameters for explicit families (Families.IsAdmissibleParam). The shared hypothesis used by the family layer asserts that the integer parameter d is squarefree and d \ne 1, matching the squarefree field-entry hypothesis for the standard model \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d).

The long-term Diophantine goal is the full Baker--Heegner--Stark theorem and related quadratic-field classification results. The elementary direction — class number one for all nine Heegner numbers, via Minkowski bounds and inert primes — is now complete in the stable surface, and the full equivalence is stated (with the deep direction as sorry) in the sketch surface. The converse remains conditional on substantial future CM, ring-class-field, modular-function, or transcendence input.

Deep Baker--Heegner--Stark direction. The deep direction: a negative squarefree d with class number one must lie in the Heegner set. Conjectured by Gauss, proved by Heegner (1952), Baker (1966), and Stark (1967); to be formalized via the Cox-style route or the Baker--Stark route.

Public status of the Baker--Heegner--Stark chapter. Status summary: the nine class-number-one theorems and the packaged forward direction are complete, sorry-free, and exported from the stable surface; the full equivalence is stated in the sketch surface with only the deep direction outstanding, which remains conditional on external CM or transcendence input.

Baker--Heegner--Stark statement. For a negative squarefree d \neq 1, the field \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d) has class number one if and only if d lies in the Heegner set. The full statement lives in the sketch surface: the elementary direction is proved, and the deep direction is the remaining sorry.

Algebra equivalences as categorical isomorphisms (QuadraticFieldCat.isoOfAlgEquiv). Algebra equivalences and categorical isomorphisms are interchangeable in QuadraticFieldCat. This lets later transport statements use either the category-theoretic language or the concrete AlgEquiv API.

Irreducibility and inseparability of X^2 - t (Counterexample.polynomial_irreducible, Counterexample.polynomial_not_separable). The defining polynomial of the extension is irreducible over \mathbb{F}_2(t), and its formal derivative vanishes, so neither the polynomial nor the adjoined root is separable.

The characteristic-2 quadratic extension (Counterexample.ExtensionField). The base field is \mathbb{F}_2(t), implemented as RatFunc (ZMod 2), and the extension adjoins a root of X^2 - t. This is the classical inseparable quadratic extension used as the test case for the hypotheses in the splitting classification.
Class-group torsion data placeholder (ClassGroup.HasClassGroupTorsionData). The torsion layer is the slot for the ambient 2-torsion and ambiguous ideal classes that feed into the genus theory layer.

Class-group triviality from inert primes (classGroup_eq_one_of_forall_le_minkowskiBound_isInertIn). If every rational prime below the Minkowski bound is inert in \mathcal{O}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)), then every ideal class is trivial. The proof takes a bounded representative, checks its prime divisors using the inertness hypothesis and the splitting API, and then applies the Dedekind principality criterion.

Class-number divisibility data placeholder (ClassGroup.HasClassNumberDivisibilityData). The divisibility layer is the predicate slot for results of the form n \mid h(d), building on the genus theory layer.

Class number one from inert primes (classNumber_eq_one_of_forall_le_minkowskiBound_isInertIn). This packages the class-group triviality criterion as the numerical class-number statement h(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)) = 1.

CM and ring-class-field input for the converse. Heegner's and Cox's arguments for the converse require substantial complex multiplication and ring-class-field input (singular moduli, the modular function j, class field theory for orders). The blueprint records this as an external mathematical dependency, not a started formalization.

Continued-fraction placeholders (ContinuedFraction.HasSqrtContinuedFractionData, ContinuedFraction.PeriodData). The scaffold records the intended interface for explicit continued-fraction data attached to \sqrt d and to specific parameter families. It is the namespace slot for the future real-quadratic continued-fraction pipeline to fundamental units.
The future real-quadratic unit pipeline should connect continued fractions and Pell solutions to explicit fundamental units.

Cox-style class-number-one route. The intended proof skeleton for the converse follows the classical Cox-style story (Cox, Primes of the form x^2+ny^2, Thm. 12.34) on top of the CM/ring-class-field input, within the overall blueprint goal. It should reuse the completed discriminant, splitting, ring-of-integers, unit, and class-group-certificate layers — the same layers the forward direction already exercises — rather than duplicating coordinate arguments.

Dedekind-domain criterion for the project order \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] (isDedekindDomain_iff_mod_four_ne_one). The project model \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] is Dedekind exactly in the same branch where it is already the full ring of integers: d \not\equiv 1 \pmod 4.

The Dedekind principality criterion (Ideal.isPrincipal_of_forall_isPrime_dvd_isPrincipal). In a Dedekind domain, an ideal whose prime divisors are all principal is itself principal (by unique factorization of ideals). A local shim under Mathlib/RingTheory/DedekindDomain/, it powers the inert-primes class-number-one certificate.

Transport of Dedekind-domain structure across ring equivalences (RingEquiv.isDedekindDomain_ringOfIntegers). This lemma is another shim candidate for eventual upstream movement once its final mathlib home is chosen; it backs the project Dedekind-domain statement.

Degenerate parameters are not quadratic fields (Qsqrtd.zero_not_isField, Qsqrtd.one_not_isField). The excluded parameters are genuinely degenerate: Qsqrtd 0 has nilpotents and Qsqrtd 1 has zero divisors. These facts justify the normalized condition d \ne 1 once squarefree integer parameters are in use, complementing the nonsquare field gate.

The quadratic-field discriminant formula (discr_formula). For squarefree d \ne 1, the discriminant of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d) is d in the 1 \pmod 4 branch and 4d otherwise, combining the \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] basis discriminant and the half-integer basis discriminant with the ring-of-integers classification.

Transport of the discriminant formula to abstract quadratic fields (exists_discr_formula_of_quadraticField). The discriminant formula transports from the standard model to an abstract quadratic field once an algebra equivalence to a standard parameter is chosen, reusing the ring-of-integers transport.
The discriminant of the half-integral basis (discr_zOnePlusSqrtOverTwo_basis). The \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt d)/2] basis has discriminant d when d = 1 + 4k.
The discriminant of the \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] basis (discr_zsqrtd_basis). The \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] basis has discriminant 4d. This is the basis calculation for the non-1 \pmod 4 branch.

Concrete discriminant examples (discr_gaussian, discr_eisenstein, discr_Qsqrtd_neg_five). The library includes checks for the Gaussian, Eisenstein, and \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5}) examples, exercising the discriminant formula.
Transport of absolute discriminants across algebra equivalences (NumberField.discr_eq_of_algEquiv). This is a local upstream candidate, used by the discriminant-formula transport.

Euclidean and norm-Euclidean ring-of-integers predicates (Euclidean.IsEuclideanRingOfIntegers, Euclidean.IsNormEuclideanRingOfIntegers). The Euclidean predicate asserts a nonempty ring-of-integers EuclideanDomain structure under the squarefree hypothesis; the norm-Euclidean predicate is a placeholder for the absolute-norm refinement.
Exceptional imaginary-unit classifications. The Gaussian and Eisenstein-type edge cases are handled separately from the d<-1 statement and the half-integral imaginary statement.

Explicit class-group data placeholder (ClassGroup.HasExplicitClassGroupData). The shared entry-point predicate records that explicit class-group data is intended for an admissible parameter d. It is the predicate slot under which the future finite norm-search pipeline will land.
Explicit unit candidates in the four Pell families. The library packages the concrete solutions as nontrivial unit candidates for n^2-1, n^2+1, n^2+2, and n^2-2.
From an explicit Pell candidate to a nontrivial unit (HasExplicitUnitCandidate.exists_unit_ne_one). A completed candidate produces a unit of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] different from both 1 and -1.
Explicit nontrivial unit candidates (HasExplicitUnitCandidate). The predicate records a nonzero Pell solution of norm 1 or -1, hence a concrete candidate for a nontrivial unit of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d].

Family-level class-group data placeholder (ClassGroup.HasFamilyClassGroupData). The family layer is the slot under which Yokoi, Chowla, and Richaud-Degert parameters will run through the Minkowski layer.

Finite norm search for class groups. A future class-group pipeline should extend the inert-primes certificate to finite norm searches that also handle split and ramified small primes (computing nontrivial class groups, e.g. h(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})) = 2 from the √-5 checks) and the real quadratic branch of the Minkowski bound.

Fundamental-unit conventions for finite unit groups. In imaginary cases with only torsion units, the blueprint records the completed fundamental-unit statements for \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d], the half-integral order, and the Gaussian and Eisenstein exceptional units.

Fundamental units in real quadratic orders (IsFundamentalUnit). This is the project predicate for a generator of the infinite part of a real quadratic unit group, modulo sign and inverse ambiguity. It abstracts the Pell-equation unit description into a predicate usable across coordinate models.

Symmetries of the fundamental-unit predicate. Being fundamental is invariant under inverse, sign, and monoid equivalence, matching the classical ambiguity of a generator of the infinite cyclic part of a real quadratic unit group.

Transport of fundamental units across ring equivalences (IsFundamentalUnit.map_ringEquiv). Fundamental-unit structure transports across ring equivalences, matching the project's broader transport-first architecture and aligning with the ring-equivalence shadow of the classification.

Generator relation for equivalences of quadratic fields (Qsqrtd.ringEquiv_param_rel). The rigidity proof begins with the generator relation: an equivalence between standard models sends the square-root generator to a pure square-root coordinate, forcing the two parameters to differ by a rational square. Squarefreeness then turns this relation into equality.

Genus theory data placeholder (ClassGroup.HasGenusTheoryData). The genus-theory layer will record 2-rank information about the class group obtained from the torsion layer and the ambient splitting trichotomy.
Trace and norm of half-integer coordinates. The element (a+b\sqrt d)/2 has trace a and the expected quadratic norm formula, which is the arithmetic input for the integrality normal-form proof.

Class number one for the nine Heegner fields (classNumber_eq_one_neg1 through classNumber_eq_one_neg163). Each Heegner parameter gives class number one. For each d the numeric Minkowski estimate (with the discriminant formula as input) confines the relevant rational primes — at worst 2, 3, 5, 7 for d = -163 — and each such prime is inert, by the d \equiv 5 \pmod 8 criterion at 2 and Legendre-symbol evaluations (closed by decide) at odd primes, so the inert-primes certificate applies.

The Heegner norm-Euclidean parameter list (Euclidean.IsHeegnerEuclideanParam). The predicate captures the classical list d \in \{-1, -2, -3, -7, -11\} of imaginary-quadratic parameters whose ring of integers is conjectured (and in fact known) to be norm-Euclidean. It is a strict subset of the nine Heegner numbers.

The elementary Heegner direction (classNumber_eq_one_of_mem_heegnerSet). This is the packaged elementary direction of Baker--Heegner--Stark: every d in the Heegner set satisfies h(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)) = 1, by case analysis over the nine certified cases.
The nine Heegner numbers (heegnerSet). These are -1, -2, -3, -7, -11, -19, -43, -67, -163, packaged as a finite set of squarefree parameters for the standard model \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d).
The imaginary quadratic Minkowski bound (exists_ideal_in_class_of_norm_le_imaginary). In the imaginary case the constant is (2/\pi)\sqrt{|D|}, refining the generic representative bound.

Numeric estimates for the imaginary quadratic Minkowski bound (minkowskiBound_lt_of_neg). If 4|D| < 9n^2, then the bound is below n. The factor 9 lets every estimate run on the crude inequality \pi > 3, which suffices for all nine Heegner discriminants.
The analogous imaginary result holds in the half-integer order for parameters k \le -2, specializing the norm-based unit criterion to the d \equiv 1 \pmod 4 branch.
For d < -1, the only units of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] are \pm 1. The proof specializes the Pell-equation unit criterion to imaginary parameters.

Integer and squarefree parameter normalization (Qsqrtd_iso_squarefree_int_param). Any rational parameter can first be replaced by an integer parameter and then by a squarefree integer parameter, using rational-square rescaling. This is the normalization pipeline behind standard parameters.

Integral normal forms in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d). The proof runs through half-integer normal forms: integral elements land in the correct explicit order according to the same mod-4 branch, supplying the non-1 \pmod 4 branch and the 1 \pmod 4 branch.
A future cleanup should unify the odd-prime and two-adic splitting statements using a Kronecker-symbol formulation where that abstraction is helpful.

Kummer-Dedekind plumbing for \mathcal{O}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)). Using the monogenic generator, the counting of primes above p, the inertia degrees, and the splitting predicates are read off the modular factorization \operatorname{minpoly}_{\theta(d)} \bmod p. These bridges feed the explicit Legendre-symbol and two-adic computations in the trichotomy.

Legendre-symbol criteria for splitting and inertia (isSplit_iff_legendreSym_eq_one, isInert_iff_legendreSym_eq_neg_one). For odd primes not dividing the parameter, splitting and inertia are controlled by the Legendre symbol.

Local mathlib-candidate shims. General-purpose facts that are missing from mathlib are developed locally under QuadraticNumberFields/Mathlib/, mirroring likely upstream paths and feeding the upstream-candidate boundary.

General-purpose lemmas live first under QuadraticNumberFields/Mathlib/, are used locally, and should later move upstream to mathlib. Project-only results, such as the ring-of-integers classification and concrete examples, remain in the project. This boundary protects the public API from pretending local shims are already upstream facts.

The Minkowski bound for quadratic fields (Qsqrtd.minkowskiBound). This specializes the number-field Minkowski bound to the quadratic field \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d), using the discriminant formula as the size input.

Minkowski-bound class-group data placeholder (ClassGroup.HasMinkowskiClassGroupData). The Minkowski layer will wrap the Minkowski representative bound, the reduced ideals, and bounded prime checks into the recipe behind the inert-primes class-number-one certificate.
Minkowski representatives of ideal classes (exists_ideal_in_class_of_norm_le). Every ideal class has a representative whose norm is at most the specialized Minkowski bound.

Uniqueness of normalized squarefree parameters (Qsqrtd.param_unique). Squarefree standard parameters are unique: an algebra equivalence between Qsqrtd d₁ and Qsqrtd d₂ forces d_1 = d_2 under the normalized hypotheses.
Multiplication of Pell solutions (IsPellSolution.mul). Pell solutions multiply according to the norm multiplication law in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d].

Pell-type equations for quadratic units (IsPellSolution). The predicate IsPellSolution d n x y records the equation x^2-dy^2=n. This is the bridge between coordinate arithmetic in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] and units.

From Pell equations to units. A norm-one Pell solution gives a unit of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d], and a norm-minus-one solution does the same after applying the dedicated construction. The nonzero square-root coordinate proves the resulting unit is nontrivial.
Explicit Pell solutions for the classical families d=n^2\pm1 and d=n^2\pm2. These completed formulas provide the unit candidates used by the Richaud-Degert family nodes.

The project-owned \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] boundary (QuadraticNumberFields.Zsqrtd). The project-owned Zsqrtd model stays independent from mathlib's Zsqrtd except for the dedicated bridge file. This is project architecture, not an upstream API.

Real and imaginary quadratic fields at infinity (Qsqrtd.isTotallyReal, Qsqrtd.isTotallyComplex, Qsqrtd.isCMField). For the standard field \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d), positive d gives a totally real field, while negative d gives a totally complex field and hence a CM field.

The nonsquare criterion for \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d) to be a field (Qsqrtd.instQuadraticField). The coordinate model is a genuine quadratic field when the parameter is not a rational square. The blueprint therefore treats the nonsquare condition as the field-entry gate for Qsqrtd d, separating the quadratic-field cases from the degenerate parameters d = 0 and d = 1.

Quadratic automorphism dichotomy (Qsqrtd.algEquiv_self_eq_refl_or_star). The automorphism group of a quadratic field has the expected dichotomy: the only automorphisms of Qsqrtd d (and hence of any abstract quadratic field) are the identity and conjugation.

Quadratic conjugation as an abstract automorphism. The project packages the nontrivial involution as a QuadraticField.Conj structure on abstract fields and as the explicit star automorphism on \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d).

Even quadratic Dedekind extensions need not be separable (Counterexample.quadratic_dedekind_not_imply_separable). The \mathbb{F}_2(t)-example shows that the stronger Dedekind-domain hypotheses used before the separability step in the splitting classification still fail to force separability of the induced fraction-field extension. This pinpoints separability as a genuinely additional input to the trichotomy.

Quadratic field extensions need not be separable (isQuadraticExtension_not_imply_isSeparable). The characteristic-2 quadratic extension is a quadratic field extension that is not separable, so the bare Algebra.IsQuadraticExtension hypothesis cannot imply separability of the fraction-field extension. This is why the abstract quadratic-field interface sits over \mathbb{Q}, which forces characteristic zero.
The category of quadratic fields (QuadraticFieldCat). QuadraticFieldCat bundles fields satisfying QuadraticField and organizes isomorphisms, functors, transport, and classification.

Degree two and number-field structure (QuadraticField.finrank_eq_two). An abstract quadratic field has \mathbb{Q}-dimension two, hence is a number field. This supplies the finite-dimensional and characteristic-zero interface used by the later ring-of-integers, discriminant, and ideal-theory layers.

Standard-model characterization of quadratic fields (isQuadraticField_iff_exists_squarefree_int_param). A field over \mathbb{Q} is quadratic if and only if it is isomorphic to one of the normalized standard models, turning the existence classification into a biconditional.
The Galois group of a quadratic field as \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}. The completed equivalences identify the two automorphisms of an abstract quadratic field, and of the standard model, with ZMod 2.

The project formalizes quadratic number fields over \mathbb{Q}. Its core workflow is to classify an abstract quadratic field, move to a standard coordinate model \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d), compute there, and then transport the result back to the abstract field.

The split/inert/ramified trichotomy for quadratic primes (splitting_classification). The stable splitting API packages split, inert, and ramified behavior for primes in quadratic number fields, building on the ring-of-integers classification and the Kummer-Dedekind plumbing.

Ramification is divisibility by the discriminant (isRamified_iff_dvd_disc). For every rational prime p, the prime ramifies in \mathcal{O}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)) if and only if p divides the discriminant of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d). Combined with the discriminant formula, this yields an explicit list of ramified primes, with the two-adic criterion at p = 2 reformulated as the divisibility check.

Rational-square rescaling of quadratic fields (Qsqrtd.rescale). Multiplying the parameter by a rational square does not change the quadratic field: Qsqrtd d is algebra-equivalent to Qsqrtd (a^2 * d) for nonzero a. This is the coordinate change used to clear denominators and normalize parameters.
The real quadratic Minkowski bound (exists_ideal_in_class_of_norm_le_real). In the real case the constant is \tfrac12\sqrt{|D|}, again refining the generic representative bound.

Reduced-ideal data placeholder (ClassGroup.HasReducedIdealData). The reduced-ideal layer will provide a concrete algorithm for selecting bounded-norm representatives that refines the Minkowski representative bound when the class group is presented through reduced forms.

Richaud-Degert parameters (Families.richaudDegertD, Families.IsRichaudDegertShift). The two-parameter shape (an)^2 + ka and the canonical shift set k \in \{-4,-2,-1,1,2,4\} package the Richaud-Degert family at the predicate level. The completed a=1 unit candidates cover the k \in \{-2,-1,1,2\} shifts already.
Explicit unit candidates for the a=1 Richaud-Degert families. The theorem identifies the parameter as n^2+k and covers shifts k \in \{-2,-1,1,2\} by reusing the four Pell families.

Ring-equivalence form of the quadratic-field classification (exists_ringEquiv_qsqrtd). The classification also has a ring-equivalence shadow. This is useful when transporting invariants whose API is stated for ring equivalences rather than algebra equivalences.

Monogenic generator for \mathcal{O}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)) (Splitting.ringOfIntegersGenerator, Splitting.adjoin_generator_eq_top, Splitting.exponent_generator_eq_one). The ring-of-integers classification is upgraded to a monogenic statement: an explicit generator \theta(d), given by \sqrt d when d \not\equiv 1 \pmod 4 and by (1+\sqrt d)/2 otherwise, generates the ring of integers, with conductor exponent one and an explicit minimal polynomial. This unlocks the unconditional Kummer-Dedekind input for every prime.

The quadratic ring-of-integers classification is project-only (ringOfIntegers_classification). The ring-of-integers classification is central to this repository but is not presented as a finished mathlib theorem.
Transport of rings of integers across algebra equivalences (AlgEquiv.ringOfIntegers). This belongs to the general transport layer, underlying the ring-of-integers transport.
The ring-of-integers classification for quadratic fields (ringOfIntegers_classification). The theorem packages the non-1 \pmod 4 branch and the 1 \pmod 4 branch into one dichotomy.

Norm-one criteria for units in the two quadratic orders. The explicit integer-ring models \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] and \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt d)/2] have norm-based unit criteria, used again in the unit-theory chapter.

Transport of the ring-of-integers classification to abstract quadratic fields (exists_ringOfIntegers_classification_of_quadraticField). After the standard-model classification, the result transports through the classification by squarefree parameters.

The 1 \pmod 4 ring-of-integers branch (ringOfIntegers_equiv_zOnePlusSqrtOverTwo_of_mod_four_eq_one). If d \equiv 1 \pmod 4, then the ring of integers of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d) is equivalent to \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt d)/2].

The non-1 \pmod 4 ring-of-integers branch (ringOfIntegers_equiv_zsqrtd_of_mod_four_ne_one). If d is squarefree, d \ne 1, and d \not\equiv 1 \pmod 4, then the ring of integers of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d) is equivalent to \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d].

The sketch import surface collects work-in-progress modules such as Euclidean, class-group, continued-fraction, family, and research scaffolding. Nodes that use this surface should not be marked complete until the corresponding Lean modules are promoted to the stable import surface.

The fundamental identity g e f = 2 in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17}) (fundamental_identity). For every rational prime, the number of primes above p, the ramification index, and the inertia degree multiply to the quadratic degree. The example records the general identity and the explicit checks for 2, 3, and 17.

The real quadratic example \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17}). Since 17 \equiv 1 \pmod 4, its ring of integers is the half-integral order \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{17})/2], its field discriminant is 17, it is totally real with no complex places, its automorphism group has order two, and the suborder \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{17}] is not Dedekind.

Minkowski representatives in the real example \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17}). The specialized bound is below 3, so every ideal class has a representative of absolute norm less than 3. This exercises the real quadratic Minkowski bound.
Prime splitting in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17}). The completed example verifies: 2 splits by the d \equiv 1 \pmod 8 criterion, 3 is inert by the Legendre-symbol criterion, 13 splits, and 17 ramifies.

Bounded representatives in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5}) (SqrtNeg5.exists_ideal_in_class_of_norm_le). The \sqrt{-5} example contains concrete bounded-norm checks that exercise the imaginary Minkowski bound and the representative theorem, alongside the concrete ideal factorizations.

Ideal factorizations in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] (factorization_of_two, factorization_of_three). The \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] examples verify ideal factorizations above 2 and 3, serving as concrete tests of the ideal-primality API and the splitting classification.

The imaginary quadratic example \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5}). Since -5 \not\equiv 1 \pmod 4, its ring of integers is \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}], its discriminant is -20, it is totally complex and a CM field, it has one complex place, its automorphism group has order two, and the order \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] is Dedekind.

Minkowski representatives in the imaginary example \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5}). The specialized bound is below 3, so every ideal class has a representative of absolute norm less than 3, complementing the explicit splitting table and the ideal factorizations.
Prime ideals in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]. The example proves primality for the explicit ideals above 2 and 3, supplying the local prime factors used in the ideal factorizations.

Ramification and inertia data above 2 and 3 in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5}). The completed quotient computations identify the ramification indices and inertia degrees of the concrete prime ideals appearing in the factorizations.
Prime splitting in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5}). The completed table records ramification at 2 and 5, splitting at 3 and 7, and inertia at 11, exercising all branches of the quadratic splitting trichotomy.

The squarefree integer hypothesis for quadratic fields (not_isSquare_ratCast_of_squarefree_ne_one). For integer parameters, the preferred hypothesis package is [Fact (Squarefree d)] [Fact (d ≠ 1)]. These assumptions imply that (d : ℚ) is not a rational square, so they provide the standard way to turn Qsqrtd (d : ℚ) into a field via the nonsquare field gate.

Classification by the squarefree-parameter functor. The standard-model functor from normalized squarefree parameters is essentially surjective on quadratic fields, and algebra-equivalent standard models have the same normalized parameter.

The discrete parameter space of normalized squarefree integers (SqfreeParam). This packages a squarefree integer d \ne 1, attaches the standard field \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d), and organizes these models as a discrete category mapping into the category of quadratic fields.

The stable public import surface contains the completed, sorry-free library: standard models, abstract quadratic-field infrastructure, ring-of-integers and discriminant classifications, splitting results, units, and examples. It builds on the project architecture.

The standard quadratic field \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d) (Qsqrtd). This is implemented as Qsqrtd d := QuadraticAlgebra ℚ d 0. An element has real and square-root coordinates, and the generator satisfies \sqrt d^2 = d. This is the computational model used for trace, norm, conjugation, discriminants, and splitting calculations.

Standard quadratic fields as categorical objects (QuadraticFieldCat.ofQsqrtd). The standard models become objects of QuadraticFieldCat via QuadraticFieldCat.ofQsqrtd, and the forgetful functor to AlgCat ℚ keeps transport compatible with ordinary \mathbb{Q}-algebra maps.

Normalized squarefree parameters for abstract quadratic fields (IsStandardParameter). A standard parameter is a squarefree integer d \ne 1 together with an algebra equivalence from the abstract field to Qsqrtd d. It records that an abstract field has been put into a normalized coordinate chart.

Baker--Stark transcendence input. The alternative Baker--Stark route needs analytic/transcendence ingredients (linear forms in logarithms, L-function estimates). Like the CM input, this is an external assumption at this stage.

Blueprint nodes use explicit tags: complete only for existing Lean declarations, partial for scaffolds, future for planned mathematics, mathlib-candidate for upstreamable general facts, project-only for local APIs, and external-assumption for deferred mathematical input.

Theorem 10.4 framework (Euclidean.theorem_10_4_framework). For squarefree d < 0 with d \ne 1, the conjectural equivalence is: d lies in the Heegner-Euclidean list \iff the ring of integers is Euclidean \iff it is norm-Euclidean. The framework theorem packages the two-way biconditionals; each direction is a sorry awaiting the existing classical proofs.

Coordinate trace and norm on \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d) (Qsqrtd.trace_eq_two_re, Qsqrtd.normHom_apply). The coordinate API computes trace and norm directly in Qsqrtd d. The trace is 2 \operatorname{re}(x), and the norm homomorphisms are the bridge from coordinate calculations to ring-of-integers and unit arguments.

Trace and norm through conjugation. In a quadratic field, x+\bar x is the trace image and x\bar x is the norm image, matching the classical formulas used later for integrality, discriminants, and units.

The two-adic splitting criteria (isSplit_two_of_mod_eight_eq_one, isInert_two_of_mod_eight_eq_five). The prime 2 is handled by the expected congruences modulo 8 and modulo 4, completing the trichotomy at the even prime.
The intended lifecycle is: add a local shim, use it in the project, upstream it through a mathlib PR, then delete the local shim and migrate callers.

Yokoi and Chowla parameter shapes (yokoiD, chowlaD, yokoiTwoParameterD, chowlaShiftD). The family layer records the shapes m^2 + r, with Yokoi's m^2 + 4, Chowla's m^2 + 1, the two-parameter m^2 + 2r, and the Chowla shift m^2 + c. These names expose the parameter shapes consumed by future class-number-one targets without yet asserting the deeper number-theoretic content.

Coordinate API for the half-integral order. The order \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt d)/2] embeds into the standard field, has norm formula x^2+xy-ky^2, and recognizes half-integer coordinates by the same-parity condition.

The half-integral order \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt d)/2] (ZOnePlusSqrtOverTwo). ZOnePlusSqrtOverTwo k is the project model of \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{1+4k})/2], used in the d \equiv 1 \pmod 4 branch inside the standard quadratic field.

Coordinate API for \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d]. The project-owned order embeds injectively into \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d), has the classical norm formula N(x+y\sqrt d)=x^2-dy^2, and decomposes elements into their integer and square-root coordinates.

Membership in the explicit degree-one ideals above p (mem_span_p_one_minus_sqrtd_iff, mem_span_p_one_plus_sqrtd_iff). For primes p dividing d-1, the ideals (p,1-\sqrt d) and (p,1+\sqrt d) in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] have coordinate membership criteria.

Primality of explicit degree-one ideals (isPrime_span_p_one_minus_sqrtd, isPrime_span_p_one_plus_sqrtd). The quotient descriptions prove that both ideals are prime in the relevant concrete splitting branch.

The order \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] (Zsqrtd). This is the project-owned model of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d], sitting inside the standard quadratic field. It is not mathlib's Zsqrtd; the bridge to mathlib's model is intentionally thin and isolated.
Quotients of explicit degree-one ideals (quotEquivZModP, quotEquivZModPNeg). Those concrete ideals have quotient descriptions by \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}, which supply the primality proofs.
A coordinate element x + y\sqrt d is a unit exactly when the corresponding Pell equation has norm 1 or -1. This is the coordinate counterpart of the norm-based unit criterion.
